quests.instruction: In “Ann gave a book to a friend”, which words are normally reduced in natural speech?
quests.word: Ann gave a book to a friend
quests.textToSpeak: Ann gave a book to a friend
options: The meaning words: “gave”, “book” and “friend”
Every word equally, because English has no stress
Only the first and the last word of the sentence
The small grammar words: “a”, “to” and “a”
quests.correctAnswer: The small grammar words: “a”, “to” and “a”
quests.hint: Clap the beats of the sentence at natural speed. Which words get a clap, and which get squeezed in between?
quests.explanation: In English, words that carry the main meaning (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) are stressed, while small grammar words such as articles and prepositions are normally unstressed and reduced. So the sentence is heard as “Ann GAVE uh BOOK tuh uh FRIEND”. Hearing the weak words as quiet is what lets you follow the whole sentence.
quests.phoneticRule: Content words usually carry stress and keep their full vowels; function words are unstressed in most contexts and typically use a weak form with a reduced vowel.
quests.spokenForm: Ann gave uh book tuh uh friend

quests.instruction: In “Kim went to the market”, how is the word “to” usually pronounced?
options: As /tuː/, with a long vowel, because every word has a full vowel
As /tə/, with a short, weak vowel because the word is unstressed
As /tɒ/, with a short stressed vowel
It is dropped completely, so “went the market” is heard
quests.correctAnswer: As /tə/, with a short, weak vowel because the word is unstressed
quests.hint: Say “went to the market” quickly and notice the vowel you use in the middle word.
quests.explanation: “To” is a function word and is not normally stressed, so its vowel is reduced to a schwa: “Kim went tuh the market”. The full vowel /tuː/ appears only when the word is stressed or at the end of a phrase.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak forms replace the full vowel of a function word with /ə/, and the full form is reserved for stressed or phrase-final positions.

quests.instruction: Which words in “Bring a chair to the table” are most likely to be reduced?
quests.word: Bring a chair to the table
quests.textToSpeak: Bring a chair to the table
options: “a”, “to” and “the”: the grammar words
“Bring”, “chair” and “table”: the meaning words
Only the word “to”
None of them: all words are reduced equally
quests.correctAnswer: “a”, “to” and “the”: the grammar words
quests.hint: Ask which words you would keep if you had to send the sentence as a very short text message.
quests.explanation: The words you would keep in a short message (bring, chair, table) are the content words, and they carry the stress. The others, a, to and the, are grammar words, and they are reduced: “Bring uh chair tuh thuh table”. The same test works for any sentence you hear.
quests.phoneticRule: A quick test for weak words is the telegram test: words that would be dropped from a telegram are usually function words that take weak forms.
quests.spokenForm: Bring uh chair tuh thuh table

quests.instruction: You ask a waiter for something: “Ask for the menu.” Which spoken form of “for” is typical?
options: “for”: a full /fɔː/ with a long vowel and strong stress
“fer-the”: the /f/ is lost and only a vowel is left
“fuh”: a weak /fə/ with a short vowel
“fore”: a long vowel with a strong /r/ sound
quests.correctAnswer: “fuh”: a weak /fə/ with a short vowel
quests.hint: Say “ask for the menu” as you would to a waiter, quickly and politely. Listen to the vowel in “for”.
quests.explanation: “For” is a preposition and is normally unstressed before a consonant, so it is reduced to /fə/: “Ask fuh the menu”. Its full form /fɔː/ is kept for stress or for the end of a clause. In the British model no /r/ is pronounced before a consonant; before a vowel, as in “for it”, a linking /r/ appears.
quests.phoneticRule: The preposition “for” has the weak form /fə/ before consonants and /fər/ before vowels, and the strong form /fɔː/ when stressed or phrase-final.

quests.instruction: In “a lot of money”, what typically happens to the word “of” in “Rent costs a lot of money”?
quests.word: Rent costs a lot of money
quests.textToSpeak: Rent costs a lot of money
options: It stays a full /ɒv/, because “of” ends the idiom “a lot of”
It is reduced to /əv/, but the /v/ is released with a strong puff before “money”
It is reduced to a weak /ə/, and the /v/ may even be lost before “money”
It becomes /ɔːf/, with a stressed vowel to mark the quantity
quests.correctAnswer: It is reduced to a weak /ə/, and the /v/ may even be lost before “money”
quests.hint: Say “a lot of money” at conversation speed and listen for how much of “of” you really hear.
quests.explanation: “Of” is a weak function word, normally /əv/, and before a consonant it is often reduced to a bare /ə/: “a lot uh money”. This is the same reduction you met in “cup-a tea”. The full form /ɒv/ appears only when “of” is stressed, which is rare.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak “of” is typically /əv/, and before consonant-initial words its final /v/ is often lost, leaving only /ə/.
quests.spokenForm: Rent costs uh lot uh money

quests.instruction: Which statement fits “at” in “Meet me at the station”?
options: “at” is said /æt/ with a strong vowel, because prepositions carry stress
“at” is said /ət/ with a short, weak vowel, as an unstressed preposition
“at” is dropped completely, so it sounds like “meet me the station”
“at” is said /ɑːt/ with a long vowel to mark the place of the meeting
quests.correctAnswer: “at” is said /ət/ with a short, weak vowel, as an unstressed preposition
quests.hint: Say “meet me at the station” quickly and listen for the vowel in the third word.
quests.explanation: “At” is a function word and is not normally stressed, so its vowel is reduced to /ə/: “Meet me uht the station”. The full form /æt/ appears when it is stressed or at the end of a clause, as in “What are you looking at?”. Hearing the weak /ət/ helps you notice that a preposition is there at all.
quests.phoneticRule: Prepositions such as “at” have a weak form /ət/ in ordinary connected speech and a strong form /æt/ only under stress or in final position.

quests.instruction: In “Tea or coffee?”, how is “or” usually pronounced?
options: As a weak /ə/, so it sounds like “tea-uh coffee”
As a full /ɔː/, because it joins two choices in a question
As /ɔːr/, with a strong /r/ before “coffee”
As /ɒ/, with a short stressed vowel before “coffee”
quests.correctAnswer: As a weak /ə/, so it sounds like “tea-uh coffee”
quests.hint: Say the question as a waiter would, quickly and lightly. How much vowel is left in the middle word?
quests.explanation: “Or” is a conjunction and is usually unstressed, so it is reduced to /ə/: “Tea uh coffee?”. The strong /ɔː/ is used for emphasis, such as “tea OR coffee, not both”. Listeners who expect a full “or” can miss the word in fast speech.
quests.phoneticRule: The conjunction “or” has the weak form /ə/ (or /ər/ before a vowel) in ordinary speech and the strong form /ɔː/ when stressed.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “but” is typical in “A small but comfortable room”?
options: /bʌt/ with a full vowel, because “but” introduces a contrast
/bʌ/ with a full vowel and the /t/ dropped
/bɒt/ with a rounded vowel and extra stress
“bət”: a weak form with a short /ə/ vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “bət”: a weak form with a short /ə/ vowel
quests.hint: Say the phrase aloud and listen to the middle word, comparing its length with “small” and “comfortable”.
quests.explanation: Even though “but” signals a contrast, it is not normally stressed. It is reduced to /bət/: “small buht comfortable”. The meaning words on either side carry the beat. Contrast is shown by the stress on those words more than by the strong form of “but”.
quests.phoneticRule: The conjunction “but” has the weak form /bət/; contrast is signalled by stress on the content words rather than by the strong form of “but”.

quests.instruction: How are the two “as” words typically pronounced in “Call me as soon as you can”?
quests.word: Call me as soon as you can
quests.textToSpeak: Call me as soon as you can
options: Both as a full /æz/, because “as” is part of a fixed phrase
The first as a weak /əz/, but the last as a full /æz/ because it begins the second half
Both as a weak /əz/, with a short vowel and a /z/ at the end
Both are dropped, leaving only “soon” between “me” and “you”
quests.correctAnswer: Both as a weak /əz/, with a short vowel and a /z/ at the end
quests.hint: Count the beats in “as soon as you can”. Which words fall on the beats?
quests.explanation: In “as soon as”, the two “as” words sit on either side of the stressed word “soon”, so both are unstressed: /əz suːn əz/. The full /æz/ is rare in this phrase. Learners who expect two strong “as” sounds often miss the phrase altogether.
quests.phoneticRule: In frames such as “as … as”, both instances of “as” are normally weak (/əz/), with stress falling on the word between them.
quests.spokenForm: Call me uz soon uz you can

quests.instruction: In a quick “Ben can swim”, which clue tells you the speaker said “can” and not “can’t”?
options: “Can” has a full /æ/ vowel, while “can’t” has a weak /ə/ vowel and a silent final consonant
“Can” has a weak /kən/, while “can’t” keeps a full vowel and a final /nt/
“Can’t” is louder, so volume is the only clue
There is no difference in speech, so only context can help
quests.correctAnswer: “Can” has a weak /kən/, while “can’t” keeps a full vowel and a final /nt/
quests.hint: Listen to the vowel in the middle word and decide whether it sounds like a small “uh” or a full open vowel.
quests.explanation: In an ordinary statement, “can” is unstressed and has a weak vowel: /kən/. “Can’t” is stressed and keeps a full vowel, /kɑːnt/ in British English or /kænt/ in American English, so the two differ in vowel quality, stress and the final /t/. Listening to the vowel is more reliable than listening for the /t/ alone.
quests.phoneticRule: “Can” normally has the weak form /kən/ in affirmative sentences, whereas “can’t” keeps a full, stressed vowel; the vowel quality is the main cue.

quests.instruction: Why is “can” said /kæn/ in “Yes, I can”, but /kən/ in “I can come”?
options: At the end of a clause “can” is stressed and strong, while before another word it is weak
At the end of a sentence “can” becomes a completely different word with another meaning in English
Short answers are spoken slowly and carefully, so every word in them is strong
The /n/ is longer at the end of the sentence, so the vowel must also be full
quests.correctAnswer: At the end of a clause “can” is stressed and strong, while before another word it is weak
quests.hint: Compare the position of “can” in the two sentences: one is last, one has a verb after it.
quests.explanation: A word at the end of a clause carries the final stress, so function words such as “can” keep their strong form there: /kæn/. Before another word, “can” is unstressed and reduced: /kən/. The same word can therefore have two pronunciations, depending on its position.
quests.phoneticRule: Function words use their strong forms when stressed or in final position, and weak forms elsewhere; the position in the phrase selects the form.

quests.instruction: On a call you hear a quick “Jo can come tonight”, with a short, weak “can”. What did the speaker most likely say?
options: “Jo can’t come tonight”, because the /t/ is hard to hear
Either one: weak and strong forms sound the same in fast speech
“Jo couldn’t come tonight”, because the vowel is short
“Jo can come tonight”: a weak /kən/ signals the positive form of the verb
quests.correctAnswer: “Jo can come tonight”: a weak /kən/ signals the positive form of the verb
quests.hint: Remember the vowel clue: a weak “uh” in “can” points to one meaning, and a full open vowel to the other.
quests.explanation: A weak, short vowel /kən/ is the signature of the positive “can”. The negative “can’t” keeps a full vowel and is stressed, so a real “can’t” would sound clearly stronger. So the weak form tells you the speaker is saying “can”, even if the /t/ would be hard to hear anyway.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak /kən/ signals the affirmative; negative “can’t” is stressed with a full vowel, which makes the vowel the decisive listening cue.

quests.instruction: How is the word “do” usually pronounced in “Where do you work now?”
options: As /duː/, with a long, strong vowel, as in “Yes, I do”
As /dəʊ/, like the first note of a musical scale
As /dɒ/, with a short stressed vowel and a clear /d/
As a weak /də/, with a short unstressed vowel
quests.correctAnswer: As a weak /də/, with a short unstressed vowel
quests.hint: Say the question at conversation speed and listen to the vowel in the second word.
quests.explanation: Auxiliary “do” is unstressed in questions, so its vowel is reduced: /də/. The strong form /duː/ appears when it is stressed, as in “Yes, I DO”, or at the end of a clause. The reduction is why “Where do you work” can sound as if “do” has almost vanished.
quests.phoneticRule: Auxiliary “do” has the weak form /də/ (or /d/ before “you”) and the strong form /duː/ only when stressed or final.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “were” fits “Why were you late?”
options: /wɜː/: a long vowel with strong stress
/wɛə/: a diphthong, like the word “wear”
/wə/: a weak vowel and no /r/ sound in this phrase
/wiː/: a long vowel, like the word “we” itself
quests.correctAnswer: /wə/: a weak vowel and no /r/ sound in this phrase
quests.hint: Say “why were you late” quickly and notice how long the vowel in “were” lasts.
quests.explanation: “Were” is an unstressed verb here, so it is reduced to /wə/. The strong form /wɜː/ appears when “were” ends a clause, as in “That’s where they were”. In the British model no /r/ is pronounced, because “you” begins with a consonant sound.
quests.phoneticRule: The auxiliary or linking verb “were” has the weak form /wə/ before consonants and the strong form /wɜː/ only under stress or in final position.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “have” is typical in “Prices have gone up”?
options: /əv/: a weak form with no /h/ and a short vowel
/hæv/: a full form with a clear /h/
/hæf/: a voiceless /f/ because “gone” follows
/hev/: the vowel is stressed to show completion
quests.correctAnswer: /əv/: a weak form with no /h/ and a short vowel
quests.hint: Say the sentence the way a newsreader would, and listen to what remains of the word “have”.
quests.explanation: As an auxiliary, “have” is unstressed and is reduced to /əv/ or even /v/: “Prices uv gone up”. The strong form /hæv/ appears when “have” is a main verb or is stressed. This weak /əv/ is also the reason for the spelling mistake “should of”.
quests.phoneticRule: Auxiliary “have” loses its /h/ and its vowel quality in unstressed positions, giving /əv/ or /v/; as a main verb it keeps /hæv/.

quests.instruction: In “Who are you waiting for?”, which small word keeps its strong form?
options: “are”, because it is the verb of the question
“for”, because it ends the clause and takes final stress
“you”, because it is the pronoun that names the listener
“who”, because it opens the question and sets the topic
quests.correctAnswer: “for”, because it ends the clause and takes final stress
quests.hint: Find the last word of the question and ask what happens to a function word when nothing follows it.
quests.explanation: A function word at the end of a clause is not followed by anything, so it receives the final stress and takes its strong form: /fɔː/. In the same question “are” and “you” are weak: /ə/ and /jə/. So one sentence can contain several weak words and one strong function word.
quests.phoneticRule: Prepositions stranded at the end of a clause (as in wh-questions) keep their strong forms because they carry the final stress.

quests.instruction: Why is “to” said /tuː/ in “Ben doesn’t want to”, but /tə/ in “Ben wants to go”?
options: The word “to” changes its meaning when it comes at the end of a clause
At the end of a clause “to” carries stress and is strong; before a verb it is weak
Negative sentences use strong forms for every function word they contain, not only for “to”
The /t/ is released more strongly after “doesn’t”, which makes the vowel full
quests.correctAnswer: At the end of a clause “to” carries stress and is strong; before a verb it is weak
quests.hint: Compare what follows “to” in each sentence: a verb in one, nothing in the other.
quests.explanation: At the end of a clause “to” stands for a missing verb and carries the final stress, so it keeps its full vowel: /tuː/. In “wants to go”, “to” is followed by a verb and is unstressed: /tə/. Position and stress, not the meaning of the word, decide which form you hear.
quests.phoneticRule: A function word that is stressed because it is clause-final reverts to its strong form, whereas the same word before a following verb is weak.

quests.instruction: A colleague says Jo wasn’t at the meeting. You reply, “Jo was there!” How is “was” pronounced?
options: As a weak /wəz/, as in the neutral sentence “Jo was tired”
As /wɜːz/, with an /r/-coloured vowel like American “were”
As a strong /wɒz/, because it carries contrastive stress in the reply
As /wɒs/, with a voiceless final consonant to sound firm
quests.correctAnswer: As a strong /wɒz/, because it carries contrastive stress in the reply
quests.hint: You are correcting what your colleague said. Which word carries that correction?
quests.explanation: Emphasis restores a function word’s strong form. In “Jo WAS there”, the speaker stresses “was” to contradict a negative statement, so the vowel is full: /wɒz/. In neutral speech it would be weak: /wəz/. Listening for stress lets you tell neutral statements from corrections.
quests.phoneticRule: Contrastive stress converts a normally weak function word into a stressed word with its strong form.

quests.instruction: How is “them” usually pronounced in “Show them the map”?
options: As a weak /ðəm/ or /əm/, with a short vowel, often without /ð/
As a full /ðem/ with a clear stressed vowel and a fully pronounced /ð/ at the start
As /ðiːm/, like the word “theme” with a long vowel
As /hem/, with an /h/ added at the start of the word
quests.correctAnswer: As a weak /ðəm/ or /əm/, with a short vowel, often without /ð/
quests.hint: Say “show them the map” quickly and listen to the vowel in “them”.
quests.explanation: “Them” is an unstressed pronoun and normally has a weak vowel: /ðəm/ or, in casual speech, just /əm/. The strong /ðem/ appears when the word is stressed, as in “not me, THEM”. Recognising “’em” helps you hear spoken English as more connected.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed object pronouns use weak forms with /ə/ and may lose their initial consonant in casual speech, as with “them” → /əm/.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “us” fits “Send us a message”?
options: “us” with a full /ʌs/ and clear stress on the pronoun itself
“uz” with a voiced /z/ at the end of the pronoun
“ass” with the vowel /æ/ and a hard /s/ at the end
“əs”: a weak /əs/ that links to “send”: “sen-dəs”
quests.correctAnswer: “əs”: a weak /əs/ that links to “send”: “sen-dəs”
quests.hint: Say “send us a message” as one smooth chunk and notice where the /d/ of “send” ends up.
quests.explanation: “Us” is an unstressed pronoun, so its vowel is weak: /əs/. Because it begins with a vowel, the /d/ of “send” links to it: “sen-dəs”. So the weak form and the linking work together to make the pronoun almost invisible.
quests.phoneticRule: The weak form /əs/ of “us” begins with a vowel, so a preceding consonant links onto it.

quests.instruction: In a quick “Let them in”, a listener can mishear “him” and “them”. Which clue separates the two reduced forms?
options: The final consonant: “him” ends in /n/
The vowel: “him” is /ɪm/, while “them” is /əm/
The first sound: “them” keeps a clear /ð/ in every phrase
There is no difference once the first sound is lost
quests.correctAnswer: The vowel: “him” is /ɪm/, while “them” is /əm/
quests.hint: Imagine both words with their first sound removed, and think about what is left that could still differ.
quests.explanation: In casual speech both pronouns can lose their first sound, leaving /ɪm/ for “him” and /əm/ for “them”. The two differ in the vowel: a short /ɪ/ in “him” and a schwa in “them”. Listening for that vowel, together with the context, helps you decide which pronoun was said.
quests.phoneticRule: When initial /h/ and /ð/ are both omitted, the pronouns “him” and “them” differ only in vowel quality (/ɪm/ versus /əm/).

quests.instruction: In “He said he would help”, which /h/ is most likely to be dropped in casual speech?
options: The first /h/, at the start of the sentence
Both /h/ sounds equally
The second /h/, in the middle of the sentence, after another word
Neither: the /h/ of “he” is kept in every position
quests.correctAnswer: The second /h/, in the middle of the sentence, after another word
quests.hint: Think about where an unstressed word sits: after a word that carries stress, or at the very start of the sentence.
quests.explanation: Pronoun /h/ is lost mainly when the pronoun follows another word and is unstressed: “said ’e would”. At the start of a sentence the pronoun usually takes some stress and keeps its /h/: “He said…”. So the position decides.
quests.phoneticRule: In weak forms, /h/ is omitted in unstressed pronouns and auxiliaries that follow another word, but is normally retained at the beginning of an utterance.

quests.instruction: In “Guests have already left”, how is “have” most likely pronounced, compared with “Have you left?” at the start of a question?
options: Mid-sentence it is /əv/ without /h/, while the question-initial one keeps its /h/
Both forms drop the /h/, because “have” is weak in every position
Both keep a clear /h/, because “have” is a content word
Mid-sentence it keeps its /h/ clearly, but the question-initial “have” drops its /h/ instead
quests.correctAnswer: Mid-sentence it is /əv/ without /h/, while the question-initial one keeps its /h/
quests.hint: Compare the position of “have” in the two sentences: after another word, or at the very start.
quests.explanation: After a stressed word, the auxiliary “have” is unstressed and loses its /h/: “Guests uv already left”. At the start of a question it is the first word of the utterance and usually keeps its /h/: “Have you left?”. Both are normal; the position decides.
quests.phoneticRule: Auxiliary “have” drops /h/ when it follows another word and is unstressed, and keeps /h/ at the start of an utterance.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “his” fits “Anna found his keys”?
options: “hiz”: a full /hɪz/ with a clear /h/ and a stressed vowel
“hiss”: the /z/ is devoiced into /s/ and the /h/ is kept
“ez”: a full vowel /e/ replaces the /ɪ/ of “his”, and the /h/ is dropped as well
“iz”: a weak /ɪz/ with no /h/, so the /d/ of “found” links to it
quests.correctAnswer: “iz”: a weak /ɪz/ with no /h/, so the /d/ of “found” links to it
quests.hint: Say “found his keys” as one chunk and listen to how the word “his” begins.
quests.explanation: “His” is an unstressed possessive, so it often loses its /h/ and its vowel is short: /ɪz/. Because it then begins with a vowel, the /d/ of “found” links onto it: “foun-diz keys”. So dropping /h/ and linking happen together.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed possessive “his” commonly drops /h/ after another word, and the resulting vowel-initial form takes the preceding consonant by linking.

quests.instruction: How is “the” usually pronounced in “Catch the bus today”?
options: /ðiː/ with a long vowel, because “bus” is a stressed noun
/ðə/: a weak “thuh” before a consonant
/zə/ with a /z/ at the start
/ðʌ/ with a stressed short vowel
quests.correctAnswer: /ðə/: a weak “thuh” before a consonant
quests.hint: Look at the first sound of the word after “the”. Is it a consonant or a vowel?
quests.explanation: Before a consonant sound, “the” is normally /ðə/, with a weak vowel: “catch thuh bus”. Before a vowel sound it changes to /ði/, which you will hear in the next question. The form of “the” therefore depends on the first sound of the next word.
quests.phoneticRule: The definite article has the weak form /ðə/ before consonant sounds and /ði/ before vowel sounds, regardless of the spelling.

quests.instruction: Why is “the” in “Park outside the office” usually /ði/ rather than /ðə/?
options: “Office” is a longer word than “bus”, so “the” needs a stronger vowel
The word “the” changes its meaning before nouns that name places or buildings
A vowel follows, so /ði/ keeps the two vowels apart, often with a small /j/ glide
/ðə/ cannot be pronounced before a vowel at all, because of a strict rule of English grammar
quests.correctAnswer: A vowel follows, so /ði/ keeps the two vowels apart, often with a small /j/ glide
quests.hint: Compare the first sound of “office” with the first sound of “bus” in the previous question.
quests.explanation: “Office” begins with a vowel sound, so “the” takes the form /ði/ to separate the two vowels: “thee office”, with a light /j/ glide as you learned in Stage 2. The change is about sound, not grammar, so it applies to “the egg”, “the hour” and “the answer” alike.
quests.phoneticRule: Before vowel-initial words “the” is /ði/, and the vowel + vowel boundary is typically bridged by a light /j/ glide.

quests.instruction: Which pronunciation of “the” fits “Pass me the eggs”?
options: /ði/, with a /j/ glide into “eggs”: “thee-yeggs”
/ðə/, the same weak form used before a consonant
/ðə/ with an /r/ link: “thuh-reggs”
/θiː/ with a voiceless first sound
quests.correctAnswer: /ði/, with a /j/ glide into “eggs”: “thee-yeggs”
quests.hint: Check the first sound of “eggs”, then recall which form of “the” goes with it.
quests.explanation: “Eggs” begins with a vowel sound, so “the” is /ði/: “Pass me thee-yeggs”. The glide /j/ often appears between the two vowels. If the next word were “pan”, you would hear the weak /ðə/ instead.
quests.phoneticRule: The choice between /ðə/ and /ði/ is decided by the following sound, and is stable across nouns of all kinds.

quests.instruction: At a shop counter an assistant says “Can I help you?” Which pronunciation of the first two words is typical?
options: “kæn ai”: a full /kæn/ with strong stress and a pause after it
“kɑːnt ai”: the negative form, with a final /t/
“kɛn ai”: a half-strong vowel with a pause after it
“kənai”: a weak /kən/ that links to “I”, with a short unstressed vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “kənai”: a weak /kən/ that links to “I”, with a short unstressed vowel
quests.hint: Say the sentence as a busy assistant would, quickly and politely, and notice which of the first words carry the beat.
quests.explanation: In a polite offer, “can” is unstressed and reduced to /kən/, and it links to the vowel of “I”: “kuhn-ai help you”. The beats fall on “help” and the meaning of the offer. Listening for this pattern helps you understand service questions at normal speed.
quests.phoneticRule: In polite offers the modal “can” and the pronoun “I” are both unstressed, so “can” takes its weak form and links onto “I”.

quests.instruction: Which words in “Pay for it at the till” are weak, and which are strong?
quests.word: Pay for it at the till
quests.textToSpeak: Pay for it at the till
options: All six words are strong, because each one is spoken separately and clearly
Only “for” and “the” are weak; “it” and “at” are strong
“for”, “it”, “at” and “the” are weak; “pay” and “till” are strong
“pay” and “till” are weak because they are short words
quests.correctAnswer: “for”, “it”, “at” and “the” are weak; “pay” and “till” are strong
quests.hint: Apply the telegram test: which words would you keep if you could send only two?
quests.explanation: “Pay” and “till” carry the meaning and take the stress. “For”, “it”, “at” and “the” are function words and are reduced: “Pay fuh-rit uht thuh till”. Notice that “for it” also takes a linking /r/ in the British model. Sorting words into strong and weak is the core skill of this stage.
quests.phoneticRule: In a short sentence the stressed words are the content words, and the remaining function words use their weak forms.

quests.instruction: Which version of “Is there a bank near here?” is the natural spoken form?
quests.word: Is there a bank near here
quests.textToSpeak: Is there a bank near here
options: Every word is said with a full vowel at the same strength
“there” is /ðə/ and “a” is /ə/, while “bank” and “here” are the stressed words
“bank” is weak and “there” is strong, because “there” points to a place
Only “is” is weak; every other word is stressed
quests.correctAnswer: “there” is /ðə/ and “a” is /ə/, while “bank” and “here” are the stressed words
quests.hint: Find the two content words and the two function words, then decide which should be louder.
quests.explanation: The content words “bank” and “here” carry the stress, while “there” and “a” are weak: /ðə/ and /ə/ (with a linking /r/ before a vowel when it follows “is”). Said this way the question flows at natural speed. Reading every word at full strength is slow and can make listeners lose the rhythm.
quests.phoneticRule: Natural questions place stress on content words and reduce function words such as “there” and “a”, which gives English its stress-timed rhythm.
